lessons.title: Function Basics
lessons.content: Functions are declared with fun, and every function has a type. Real scenario: extracting repeated validation logic across three screens into a single reusable function.

lessons.title: Function Parameters
lessons.content: Parameters are typed and immutable (val) by default inside the function body. Real scenario: a List<Item> parameter can't be accidentally reassigned mid-function, only mutated if it's a MutableList.

lessons.title: Return Types
lessons.content: A function's return type is written after the parameter list; Unit can be omitted. Real scenario: declaring Result<User> explicitly so every caller knows to handle success and failure at compile time.

codeSnippets.code:
fun fetchUser(id: String): Result<User> = TODO()
fun logEvent(name: String) { println("Event: $name") }

lessons.title: Default Arguments
lessons.content: Parameters can have default values, letting callers omit them - eliminating most need for overloading. Real scenario: a network function with a default 30s timeout that a slow upload endpoint can override.

codeSnippets.code:
fun fetchData(url: String, timeoutMs: Long = 30_000): String = TODO()
fetchData("https://api.example.com")
fetchData("https://api.example.com/upload", 120_000)

lessons.title: Named Arguments
lessons.content: Named arguments let you specify parameters by name, improving readability and letting you skip earlier defaults. Real scenario: calling a function with several boolean flags where named args make each one unambiguous.

codeSnippets.code:
fun createUser(name: String, isAdmin: Boolean = false, isVerified: Boolean = false) {}
createUser(name = "Alice", isVerified = true)

lessons.title: Single-Expression Functions
lessons.content: When a function body is a single expression, use = instead of { return }. Real scenario: small pure utility functions read more like math notation and are quicker to scan in review.

codeSnippets.code:
fun square(x: Int) = x * x
fun isEven(n: Int) = n % 2 == 0

lessons.title: Local (Nested) Functions
lessons.content: You can define a function inside another function, with access to the enclosing function's variables. Real scenario: extracting a small validation helper only needed inside one specific function.

lessons.title: Infix Functions
lessons.content: A function marked infix can be called without the dot and parentheses, reading like an operator - must have exactly one parameter. Real scenario: this is how Kotlin's own 'to' (Pairs) reads naturally.

lessons.title: Tail-Recursive Functions
lessons.content: Marking a function tailrec lets the compiler optimize a tail-position recursive call into a loop, avoiding stack overflow. Real scenario: implementing factorial recursively for very large inputs safely.

codeSnippets.code:
tailrec fun factorial(n: Long, acc: Long = 1): Long =
    if (n <= 1) acc else factorial(n - 1, n * acc)

lessons.title: Extension Functions
lessons.content: Extension functions add new functions to existing classes without inheritance or modifying the original source. Real scenario: adding isValidEmail() on String throughout your codebase.

codeSnippets.code:
fun String.isValidEmail(): Boolean = contains("@") && contains(".")
val valid = "user@example.com".isValidEmail()

lessons.title: Higher-Order Functions
lessons.content: A higher-order function takes another function as a parameter or returns one - the foundation of map/filter and callback APIs. Real scenario: a reusable retry() utility taking the operation as a lambda.

lessons.title: Lambda Expressions
lessons.content: A lambda is an anonymous function literal: { params -> body }. If it's the last parameter, it moves outside the parentheses (trailing lambda syntax). Real scenario: filtering lessons by tag with a one-line lambda.

lessons.title: Anonymous Functions
lessons.content: An anonymous function has explicit return type and local-only return semantics, unlike a lambda's non-local return. Real scenario: needing a function parameter where return shouldn't exit the outer calling function.

lessons.title: Function Types
lessons.content: A function type like (Int, Int) -> Int describes a function's shape and can be used as a variable/parameter/return type. Real scenario: a strategy pattern swapping calculation strategies at runtime.

codeSnippets.code:
var operation: (Int, Int) -> Int = { a, b -> a + b }
operation = { a, b -> a * b }

lessons.title: Closures
lessons.content: A lambda can capture variables from its enclosing scope, including mutating a var directly. Real scenario: a counter closure remembering state across multiple invocations for a debouncing utility.

lessons.title: Recursion
lessons.content: A recursive function calls itself to break a problem into smaller sub-problems, with a base case. Real scenario: traversing a nested comment thread or file directory tree of unknown depth.
